overview: The file documents Japan’s July–August 1932 reorganization of its authority in Manchuria by consolidating military, civil, and diplomatic powers under one senior official. Cross-reference sheets and telegrams from Nelson T. Johnson in Peiping and Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo trace the Cabinet decision, the anticipated selection and eventual installation of General Nobuyoshi Mutō as commander-in-chief, governor of the Kwantung Leased Territory, and special plenipotentiary, and the appointment of Hirotarō Hayashi to lead the South Manchuria Railway. The correspondence also records the planned headquarters at Changchun, Japanese efforts to deny that the new post implied formal recognition of Manchukuo, a protest by the Chinese minister, and General Shigeru Honjō’s reassignment to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Chinese Legation letter on a plenipotentiary for Manchuria
subfiles.about: The sheet refers researchers to a Chinese Legation letter concerning Japan’s proposed consolidation of authority in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The filing note points to document 893.01 Manchuria/355. The referenced letter concerns the Japanese Government’s appointment of an envoy extraordinary and plenipotentiary who would also serve as commander-in-chief and governor-general of Kwantung.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Johnson telegram No. 856
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a telegram reporting the Japanese Cabinet’s decision to create a powerful special envoy for Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The note directs researchers to telegram No. 856 in file 893.01 Manchuria/354. It summarizes the decision that the commander-in-chief should appoint a plenipotentiary who would be governor of Kwantung and exercise control over the South Manchuria Railway.

subfiles.title: Johnson telegram on the Japanese administrative reorganization in Manchuria
subfiles.about: Johnson relays a Reuter report on the Cabinet plan to unify Japanese administration in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The Cabinet decided that the commander-in-chief would provisionally appoint a special envoy with plenipotentiary powers who would also govern Kwantung. Acting under the foreign minister, the envoy would supervise Japanese consuls and foreign affairs in Manchuria. General Nobuyoshi Mutō was expected to receive the post, while Hirotarō Hayashi was chosen as president of the South Manchuria Railway.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Grew telegram No. 203
subfiles.about: The sheet references Grew’s report on the consolidation of three major Japanese offices in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The filing note directs researchers to telegram No. 203 in file 893.01 Manchuria/361. It identifies the subject as the Cabinet decision to combine the Kwantung garrison command, the governor-generalship of the leased territory, and the special plenipotentiary’s office.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on consolidated Japanese authority in Manchuria
subfiles.about: Grew explains the powers, expected occupant, legal basis, and diplomatic implications of Japan’s new supreme office in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the Cabinet combined military command, civil government, and diplomatic supervision in one post answerable respectively to the War Office, Department of Overseas Affairs, and Foreign Office. The official would outrank other Japanese authorities in Manchuria, establish headquarters at Changchun, and was expected to be General Nobuyoshi Mutō; the system was expected to take effect on August 5 or 6. The Foreign Office argued that appointing a special plenipotentiary under the 1917 ordinance did not constitute recognition of Manchukuo, citing Viscount Ishii’s 1917 mission to the United States. The Chinese minister protested, while Grew clarified that the South Manchuria Railway would remain largely outside the new office’s direct control.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Johnson telegram No. 926
subfiles.about: The sheet references a telegram announcing General Mutō’s installation as governor of the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The filing note directs researchers to telegram No. 926 in file 893.01 Manchuria/378. Its subject entry records that General Nobuyoshi Mutō had been installed as governor of the Kwantung Leased Territory.

subfiles.title: Johnson telegram on Mutō’s installation and Honjō’s reassignment
subfiles.about: Johnson relays news of Mutō’s formal installation as the supreme Japanese authority in Manchuria and Honjō’s return to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: A Reuter report from Tokyo states that Emperor Hirohito formally installed General Nobuyoshi Mutō as supreme head of Japanese affairs in Manchuria. Mutō would simultaneously serve as army commander-in-chief, governor of the Kwantung Leased Territory, and special envoy to Manchukuo. General Shigeru Honjō, the outgoing army commander in Manchuria, would return to Tokyo as Supreme Military Councillor.

interest: The file offers a compact documentary sequence showing how Japan institutionalized unified military, colonial, and diplomatic authority in Manchuria shortly after creating Manchukuo. Particularly valuable are Grew’s detailed explanation of the new official’s divided bureaucratic responsibilities and the Foreign Office’s legal argument that a plenipotentiary could be appointed without recognizing Manchukuo. The cross-reference sheets also reveal State Department filing practices and connect the Kwantung political file to the broader Manchurian decimal-file series.
